overview.body:
**Yama** ​(*yama*) — ‌Death, the ‌First Mortal, ​Judge of ​the Dead ​· The ​god who ​presides over ‌the Pitṛs ​— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Death, Justice, ​Underworld". The ​name means ​"The god ​who presides ‌over the ​Pitṛs (the ‌departed fathers) ​and rules ‌the spirits ​of the ‌dead."[^1].

**Yama** ​is ‌death’s king ​in the ​Indian traditions: ‌the first ‌man to ‌die, who ​found the ​way to ‌the fathers’ ​world and ​now rules ‌it — ​and judges ​who may ‌enter. ​With his ‌noose and ​his two ​four-eyed dogs, ​he waits ​at the ‌southern direction, ‌the realm ​of the ‌ancestors, and ​his account-book ​is the ‌oldest audit ‌in human ‌literature.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as **Yama** ​and serves ​its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/yama/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form *yama* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Devanagari ​as ​**यम**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"The ​god ​who presides ‌over ​the ‌Pitṛs ​(the departed ‌fathers) ​and ​rules ​the ​spirits of ​the ‌dead."[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*yama* ‌survives ​only ‌because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system ​could ‌not carry ‌diacritics; ‌it ​is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Yama** ‌recovers the ​full ​diacritic ​detail ​of ‌the scholarly ‌transliteration ​directly ‌in ​the address ​bar. ‌The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ​a ‌description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**y** ​→ ​**Y** — ‌Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ​**a** — ‌Short ​/a/
- ‌**m** ‌→ **m** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** ​→ ‌**a** — ‌Short ​/a/

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈjʌmə/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Yama).[^1]

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Ya-** ​— Palatal ‌y ​as ‌in ​“young”; the ​a ​is ​short and ​open.
- ‌**-ma** ​— ‌The name ​means ‌“twin” ​— ‌Yama is ​the ‌twin ​of Yamī ​in ‌the ‌earliest ‌tradition.
- **Yam-** ​— ​In ‌compound ​names the ​stem ‌surfaces ​as yam- ​— ‌the ​river ‌Yamunā preserves ​his ​twin ​sister’s ​name.

For ‌the ‌modern ​speaker, the ‌closest ​approximation ​is: ‌“YUM-uh”

Kindred ‌and ‌historical ‌forms ​of the ‌name:

- ​**Avestan** ​— Yima
- ​**Vedic** ‌— ​Yamī ​(his twin ​sister)
- ‌**Buddhist** ​— ​Yama/Enma

The ​lord ‌of ​the dead ‌was ​the ‌first ​mortal — ‌the ‌one ​who ​found the ​path ​and ‌guards it ‌ever ​since.

domains.body:
**Yama** ​is death’s ‌king ‌in the ​Indian traditions: ​the ​first man ​to ​die, who ‌found the ​way ​to the ‌fathers’ ​world and ‌now ​rules it ‌— and ​judges ​who may ​enter. ​With his ​noose ‌and his ​two four-eyed ‌dogs, ​he waits ‌at ​the southern ‌direction, the ​realm ‌of the ​ancestors, ​and his ‌account-book ‌is the ‌oldest audit ​in ​human literature.[^1]

### ‌The ​First Mortal

​He ‌died before ​anyone — ​the ‌twin who ​found ‌the path ​to the ​fathers ​and became ​its ‌king.

### The ‌Noose

​His pāśa, ‌the noose, ​finds ​every soul ‌at ‌its hour; ‌none ‌outrun it, ​though all ‌may ​beg.

### The ​Two ​Dogs

Śyāma ‌and Śabala, ​four-eyed, ​follow his ​road ‌and report ​the ​dead; they ​guard the ‌way.

### ​Judge of ‌the ​Deeds

In ‌the ​Mahābhārata and ‌Purāṇas he ‌reads ​the record ​of ​every soul ​— the ‌karma, ‌weighed without ​scales.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Yama ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set ‌of recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed ‌statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​First ​Mortal** ​— ​He died ‌before ​anyone ‌— ​the ‌twin who ​found ‌the ​path ‌to ​the ​fathers and ‌became ‌its ‌king.
- ​**The ​Noose** ‌— His ​pāśa, ​the ‌noose, ​finds ​every ‌soul at ​its ‌hour; ​none ​outrun ​it, ​though all ‌may ‌beg.
- ​**The ‌Two ​Dogs** ​— Śyāma ‌and ‌Śabala, ‌four-eyed, ‌follow ​his ‌road and ​report ​the ​dead; ‌they ​guard the ​way.
- ​**Judge ‌of ​the ​Deeds** ​— In ‌the ​Mahābhārata ‌and ​Purāṇas ‌he ​reads the ‌record ‌of ​every ​soul ​— ​the karma, ‌weighed ‌without ​scales.

mythology.body:
Yama’s mythology ​moves from Vedic ‌pathfinder to epic judge ‌to Purāṇic king ​of hells. He ​begins as the twin ​who chose to ​die — the ​first of the race ‌to walk the ​path — and ​becomes the stern ‌accountant whose city the ​dead enter by ‌the southern gate. ​Buddhism and the epics ‌gave him his ​tortures and his ​buffalo; the Veda ​kept his dignity.[^1]

### The ​Twin Dialogue (Rigveda ​10.10)

The oldest ‌Yama-text is a dialogue: ​Yama and his ‌twin Yamī, the ​first two beings, and ‌Yamī’s love for ​her brother. Yama ‌refuses — ‘the ​immortals watch’ — and ‌the hymn becomes ​the charter of ​exogamy and of the ‌incest-taboo itself, argued ‌between the world’s ‌first twins in ​the world’s first debate.[^2]

### ​The Path of ‌the Fathers (Rigveda ​10.14)

The funeral hymn ​sends the dead ‌king along the ​path Yama blazed, past ​the two dogs ‌and the waters, ​to the feast ‌of the fathers where ​Yama waits with ​Varuṇa. ‘Leave the ​sin here, keep the ​glory’ — the ‌formula of every ‌Vedic funeral, spoken to ​the first traveller’s ‌successor.

### The King ​Under the Earth ​(Mahābhārata)

In the epic’s ‌underworld-book, Yama rules ‌below with his ‌city Saṃyamanī, his account ‌read by Citragupta, ​his noose and ‌his buffalo — ​the god of justice ​who once disguised ​himself as a ‌crab to test a ​king. The epic ​makes him dreaded ​and fair: the judge ‌who cannot be ​bribed because he ​already owns everything.

### ​The Lord of the ‌Narakas (Purāṇic Hell)

​The Purāṇas enumerate ‌eighty-four hells under Yama’s ​administration, each a ‌precise torment for ​a precise sin ‌— the liar’s tongue, ‌the thief’s hands. ​Yet the same ​texts insist his justice ​is karma’s arithmetic, ​not malice: even ‌the tortures are purification, ‌and release comes ​in time.

syncretism.body:
The ​Avestan ‌Yima, ‌king ​of ​the ​golden age ​who ​kept ‌death ​from ​his ‌realm, ​is ‌Yama’s ​Iranian ‌twin ​— ​the ​same name, ​opposite ​function: ‌where ​Yima ‌postponed ​death, ‌Yama ​administers ‌it. ​Buddhism ‌made ​Yama a ​dharmapāla, ‌converted ‌in ‌the ​end ​by ‌the ​Buddha’s ​teaching, ‌and ​carried ​him ‌east as ​Enma ‌in ​Japan, ​where ​he ​still ‌judges ‌with ​his ‌mirror ​and ​staff.[^1]

‌Kindred figures ‌in ‌the ‌PuniCodex ​cross-tradition ‌index ​include ​[[hades|Hádēs]] ​(underworld ‌/ ​death), ​[[anubis|ꜣnpw]] ​(underworld / ‌death), ​[[cerberus|Kérberos]] ​(underworld ​/ ‌death), ​[[ereshkigal|Ereškigal]] ‌(underworld ​/ ‌death), ​[[forseti|Forseti]] ‌(justice ‌/ ​law / ​truth), ​and ​[[garmr|Garmr]] ‌(underworld ‌/ ​death).

vedic-references.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Yama. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with death.

The IAST restoration Yama marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]

upanishads.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Yama appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Yama carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]

puranas.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Yama in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Yama is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]

mantras.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Yama encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Yama preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
